While early ascertainment suggested a uniform, recognizable presentation, recent cohort expansions encompassing at least 68 to 69 cumulative individuals across international series have revealed significant variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance [F1, F2, F18]. --- ## 1. Phenotypic Spectrum and Documented Clinical Frequencies Identifying an individual with Fliedner-Zweier syndrome from clinical phenotype alone is exceptionally difficult because its core features overlap broadly with common neurodevelopmental presentations [F2, F5]. Discriminative Features and Clinical Differential Diagnosis Bedside differentiation of Fliedner-Zweier syndrome solely on clinical criteria is **not achievable with moderate or high clinical confidence**, and the confidence of bedside distinction without sequencing is very low [F2, F15]. Fliedner-Zweier syndrome exhibits extensive phenotypic pleiotropy: affected individuals present with non-specific developmental delay, a wide cognitive spectrum (from completely normal IQ or borderline intellectual disability to severe ID), variable speech delay, behavioral abnormalities (ADHD, autism spectrum traits), skeletal anomalies, and seizures [F1, F2, F4, F5]. ### Confused Overlapping Disorders and Confidence of Distinction 1. **Spliceosomal and Transcription-Elongation Machinery Syndromes**: - *Overlapping entities*: *SRRM1*-related neurodevelopmental disorder (Altay et al., 2026, [10.1038/s41431-025-01966-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41431-025-01966-y)), *THOC6*-related neurodevelopmental disorder, *RNU4ATAC*-related microcephalic dwarfism/syndromes, and *SCAF8*-associated conditions [F2, F15]. - *Overlapping findings*: Shared disruption of general mRNA transcription elongation and splicing creates converging clinical phenotypes involving developmental delay, speech limitations, muscular hypotonia, and non-specific skeletal anomalies [F2, F15]. - *Confidence of bedside distinction*: **Very Low (<0.30)**. Transcriptome deregulations affect thousands of downstream targets (e.g., >9,000 deregulated genes and ~2,900 differentially spliced transcripts [F2]), producing convergent neurodevelopmental disruptions that cannot be separated clinically without exome or genome sequencing [F2, F15]. 2. **Chromatin Remodeling Syndromes (e.g., Coffin-Siris Syndrome, *ARID1B* / *SMARCA4*)**: - *Overlapping findings*: Muscular hypotonia, intellectual impairment, expressive language delay, and subtle craniofacial dysmorphisms [F15]. - *Discriminating clues*: Coffin-Siris and related SWI/SNFopathies frequently show fifth-digit nail/distal phalanx hypoplasia, pronounced coarse facial coarsening, and structural internal organ malformations, whereas FZS dysmorphism remains subtle and unclassifiable [F10, F15]. - *Confidence of bedside distinction*: **Low to Moderate**. While digit hypoplasia points toward Coffin-Siris, genomic sequencing remains mandatory [F2, F15]. ### Most Discriminating Features of Fliedner-Zweier Syndrome When comparing an affected individual to patients with generic neurodevelopmental delay, the combination of features that raises suspicion includes: - **Severe expressive language delay relative to general cognitive performance**: Speech deficits are consistently penetrant even in patients who preserve mild or near-normal non-verbal cognitive capacities [F4, F7]. - **Co-occurrence of axial and lower-extremity joint positional anomalies**: Recurrent skeletal signs specifically encompass scoliosis, developmental dysplasia of the hip, and clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) [F5, F12]. - **Pharmacoresponsive focal epilepsy**: When seizures occur (median onset around 4 years of age), they often present as focal seizures responsive to standard anti-seizure medications [F9, F13]. --- ## 3. Discriminative Features and Clinical Differential Diagnosis Bedside differentiation of Fliedner-Zweier syndrome solely on clinical criteria is **not achievable with moderate or high clinical confidence**, and the confidence of bedside distinction without sequencing is very low [F2, F15]. Fliedner-Zweier syndrome exhibits extensive phenotypic pleiotropy: affected individuals present with non-specific developmental delay, a wide cognitive spectrum (from completely normal IQ or borderline intellectual disability to severe ID), variable speech delay, behavioral abnormalities (ADHD, autism spectrum traits), skeletal anomalies, and seizures [F1, F2, F4, F5]. ### Confused Overlapping Disorders and Confidence of Distinction 1. **Spliceosomal and Transcription-Elongation Machinery Syndromes**: - *Overlapping entities*: *SRRM1*-related neurodevelopmental disorder (Altay et al., 2026, [10.1038/s41431-025-01966-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41431-025-01966-y)), *THOC6*-related neurodevelopmental disorder, *RNU4ATAC*-related microcephalic dwarfism/syndromes, and *SCAF8*-associated conditions [F2, F15]. - *Overlapping findings*: Shared disruption of general mRNA transcription elongation and splicing creates converging clinical phenotypes involving developmental delay, speech limitations, muscular hypotonia, and non-specific skeletal anomalies [F2, F15]. - *Confidence of bedside distinction*: **Very Low (<0.30)**. Transcriptome deregulations affect thousands of downstream targets (e.g., >9,000 deregulated genes and ~2,900 differentially spliced transcripts [F2]), producing convergent neurodevelopmental disruptions that cannot be separated clinically without exome or genome sequencing [F2, F15]. 2. **Chromatin Remodeling Syndromes (e.g., Coffin-Siris Syndrome, *ARID1B* / *SMARCA4*)**: - *Overlapping findings*: Muscular hypotonia, intellectual impairment, expressive language delay, and subtle craniofacial dysmorphisms [F15]. - *Discriminating clues*: Coffin-Siris and related SWI/SNFopathies frequently show fifth-digit nail/distal phalanx hypoplasia, pronounced coarse facial coarsening, and structural internal organ malformations, whereas FZS dysmorphism remains subtle and unclassifiable [F10, F15]. - *Confidence of bedside distinction*: **Low to Moderate**. While digit hypoplasia points toward Coffin-Siris, genomic sequencing remains mandatory [F2, F15]. ### Most Discriminating Features of Fliedner-Zweier Syndrome When comparing an affected individual to patients with generic neurodevelopmental delay, the combination of features that raises suspicion includes: - **Severe expressive language delay relative to general cognitive performance**: Speech deficits are consistently penetrant even in patients who preserve mild or near-normal non-verbal cognitive capacities [F4, F7].

Discriminative Features and Clinical Differential Diagnosis Bedside differentiation of Fliedner-Zweier syndrome solely on clinical criteria is **not achievable with moderate or high clinical confidence**, and the confidence of bedside distinction without sequencing is very low [F2, F15]. Fliedner-Zweier syndrome exhibits extensive phenotypic pleiotropy: affected individuals present with non-specific developmental delay, a wide cognitive spectrum (from completely normal IQ or borderline intellectual disability to severe ID), variable speech delay, behavioral abnormalities (ADHD, autism spectrum traits), skeletal anomalies, and seizures [F1, F2, F4, F5].
